questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to solve a technical problem while thinking aloud with a teammate; what was your approach and how did you keep the conversation productive?
questions.not_scored_reason: A newly written practice question nobody has reviewed yet, so it is not scored — the notes show what a strong answer covers.

exchanges.text: Hi, I'm Ananya — thanks for making the time. I'm joined by Meera, and we'll keep this conversational. Hi! I'll be sitting in, and I might jump in with a question or two. Let's start with something easy. Tell me about a time you had to solve a technical problem while thinking aloud with a teammate; what was your approach and how did you keep the conversation productive?

In my third-year project we were building a REST API for a hostel complaint system and the complaints endpoint started timing out under load. My teammate and I debugged it over a call. I said out loud what I was checking at each step: first the logs, then the query, and we found it was doing a full table scan because there was no index on the status column. I kept it productive by writing down each hypothesis in a shared doc and agreeing on the next check before running it, so we never argued in circles. Adding the index brought the response time from about 4 seconds to under 100 milliseconds.
Can I jump in with one? Why does adding an index on the status column eliminate the full table scan and reduce the response time so dramatically?

Without an index the database has no way to find rows with a given status except checking every row, so the query is O(n) in the table size. A B-tree index on status keeps the keys sorted with pointers to the rows, so the lookup becomes a tree descent, O(log n), and then it reads only the matching rows. Our table had a few hundred thousand complaints and only a small fraction were open, so we went from reading everything to reading a tiny slice. The trade-off is that every insert and update now also has to update the index, and an index on a low-cardinality column helps only if the value you filter on is selective.

questions.one_strong_answer: In my internship I was debugging a memory leak in a microservice while paired with a senior engineer. I started by stating the symptom, then walked through the code path I was inspecting, vocalising each hypothesis—"maybe the connection pool isn’t closed"—and asked, "Does that align with what you saw in the logs?" He confirmed and added his observation about a recent config change. I paused after each step to let him interject, and when he suggested an alternative, I paraphrased his point to show I was listening. Together we identified an unclosed file handle, fixed it, and the service’s memory usage dropped by 30 %. The whole session lasted 20 minutes and demonstrated how thinking aloud, combined with active listening, keeps problem-solving efficient.

questions.question: Why is average-case lookup in a hash map O(1), and what has to be true for that to hold?

exchanges.text: Thanks, Meera. Nicely put. Alright — let's switch gears. Next up: Data structures and algorithms. Why is average-case lookup in a hash map O(1), and what has to be true for that to hold?
Because the hash function gives you the index directly, so you just go to that slot in the array and get the value. That is why it is constant time.
What assumptions about the hash function’s distribution and the table’s load factor are necessary to keep collisions rare enough that the expected lookup remains constant time?
Honestly I'm not sure about the assumptions. I think it just needs a good hash function?
Can you describe more precisely what “good” means for the hash function and how the load factor should be bounded to keep expected collisions low?
I don't know how the load factor should be bounded.

This holds only if the hash function distributes keys uniformly (or close to it) and the table’s load factor remains bounded—usually by resizing when it exceeds a constant threshold such as 0.75. If either condition fails, many keys collide and lookup can approach O(n).

questions.question: What does it mean for a sort to be stable?

exchanges.text: We've got about 1 minutes left — no rush. Okay, here's the next one. What does it mean for a sort to be stable?

A sort is stable if records with equal keys keep the same relative order they had in the input. For example, if I sort students by marks and two students both have 85, a stable sort keeps whoever came first in the original list first. It matters when you sort by multiple keys in passes: sort by name first, then stably by marks, and students with equal marks stay alphabetical. Merge sort and insertion sort are stable; quicksort and heapsort in their usual forms are not.
Can I jump in with one? What is actually happening underneath that makes it work?

Underneath, a stable sort never swaps two equal elements past each other. Merge sort, for example, takes from the left half when keys are equal, so earlier elements stay first. Quicksort's partition can move an equal element across the pivot, which is why it loses the order.
